chain.label: Night surface operations at STL
chain.trigger: The accident occurred at N 38°44', W 90°21', during the hours of darkness.

chain.label: Cessna pilot operating during his normal sleep period and eager to get home ahead of forecast snow
chain.trigger: the accident occurred at a time of night when the pilot normally went to sleep, and he may have been tired... he mentioned that it was going to snow in Iron Mountain

chain.label: Cessna 441 external lighting gave poor conspicuity from behind on a lighted runway; no aft-visible anticollision light and strobes customarily off until takeoff clearance
chain.trigger: The Cessna 441 was not equipped with a rotating red anticollision light, which on many other aircraft types is visible from behind the airplane... Federal standards for aircraft external lighting are primarily intended to serve in-flight conspicuity needs rather than conspicuity of aircraft on airport surfaces.

chain.label: STL practice of omitting runway 31's occasional departure use from the ATIS and not treating it as an active runway; ATIS listed only 30R/30L as active
chain.trigger: No mention was made of the occasional use of runway 31 as a departure runway in this ATIS recording... the STL controllers did not typically treat runway 31 as if it were an active runway

chain.label: Ground controller issued a nonstandard taxi clearance that omitted 'taxi to runway 31,' and no runway readback was obtained
chain.trigger: the pilot of the Cessna 441 received a nonstandard clearance, in which the phrase 'taxi to,' and the departure runway had been eliminated

chain.label: ASDE-3 surface detection radar unavailable to controllers because of a computer hard drive failure
chain.trigger: The ASDE-3 equipment was not available on the night of the accident because the computer hard drive had failed.

chain.label: Cessna pilot's mistaken belief that runway 30R was his assigned departure runway; he did not register the clearance to runway 31
chain.trigger: the Cessna 441 pilot's mistaken belief that his assigned departure runway was runway 30R

caused_by.evidence: The combination of the time of day and his desire to return home before the weather deteriorated may have contributed to the mistaken actions of the Cessna 441 pilot

if runway 31 had been referenced as a runway for occasional general aviation departures on the ATIS broadcast, the pilot may have been more attentive to the controller's taxi clearance and runway assignment
Had the taxi clearance been in accordance with prescribed phraseology, it might have altered the pilot's preconception of departing on runway 30R.

chain.label: Cessna deviated from its taxi clearance and taxied via taxiway Romeo into takeoff position on active runway 30R at an intersection, without clearance
chain.trigger: the pilot of the Cessna 441 unintentionally deviated from the taxi clearance he received from the ground controller and taxied onto the active runway being used by the MD-82

caused_by.evidence: he had a preconception that he would be departing on runway 30R and thus did not register the ground controller's clearance to runway 31

chain.label: Cessna sitting on the runway 30R centerline for about 3 minutes went undetected by the controllers and by the MD-82 flightcrew, who were cleared for and began their takeoff roll
chain.trigger: they did not observe the airplane or airplane position lights at any point during their takeoff roll... the controllers could not have reasonably been expected to visually detect the Cessna pilot's deviation from the taxi instructions

caused_by.evidence: The airplane taxied to the intersection of taxiway Romeo and runway 30R, where it remained for about 3 minutes before the collision.

the darkness, poor conspicuity of the Cessna 441, and physical distance between the ATC tower cab and the northeast portion of the STL airport contributed to the controller's failure to see the Cessna 441 on runway 30R

the white tail cone-mounted navigation light would have blended in with the runway centerline lighting system and... it would not be reasonable to expect that the MD-82 flightcrew could have seen the Cessna 441 in time to prevent the accident

had the ASDE-3 equipment been available for controller use on the night of the accident, the ground and local controllers would have had a higher probability of identifying the Cessna 441 at runway 30R

chain.label: MD-82's right wing struck the Cessna 441 at the runway 30R / taxiway Romeo intersection during the takeoff roll; Cessna destroyed, MD-82 substantially damaged
chain.trigger: The right wing of the MD-82 struck the tail cone and fuselage structure of the Cessna 441, separating the horizontal and vertical stabilizers from the fuselage and shearing the top of the fuselage/cockpit from the airplane.

caused_by.evidence: his undetected entrance onto runway 30R, which was being used by the MD-82 for its departure
About 2 to 3 seconds after the 80-knot call, the additional crewmember... yelled 'There's an airplane!'... Approximately 2 to 3 seconds after the flightcrew saw the Cessna 441, they felt an impact

chain.label: Both Cessna occupants killed; eight MD-82 passengers minor injuries during the fuel-spill evacuation
chain.trigger: The pilot and pilot-rated passenger on board the Cessna 441 died of severe craniocerebral injuries... eight passengers sustained minor injuries during the evacuation.

caused_by.evidence: The headrests on cabin and cockpit seats on the Cessna 441 were separated or bent forward, at the same level that the upper cabin structure was sheared off. This accident was not survivable for the occupants of the Cessna.
